newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: MEDIA INQUIRY MAY BITE THE DUST

There's mounting speculation that Federal Cabinet will today formally decide to abandon its promised media ownership inquiry. The Coalition promised during the election campaign to hold a full inquiry into existing cross-media ownership rules, as well as restrictions on foreign ownership of Australian media outlets.
However there's speculation the inquiry will be ditched in favour of a Government discussion paper, outlining alternative media regulations.
Communications Minister Richard Alston refused to be drawn over the speculation as he entered the Cabinet meeting.
ANSETT APPOINTS NEW SAFETY HEAD AFTER REPORT
A report by the Bureau of Air Safety Investigation released today has found Ansett training procedures were inadequate at the time of a crash-landing of an aircraft in Sydney, almost two years ago.
The B-747 aircraft was an hour into its journey from Sydney to the Japanese city of Osaka when the number one engine was shut down due to an oil leak.
The flight was aborted and the crew prepared for landing in Sydney but experienced problems with the hydraulic system, which did not allow the nose wheel to extend in time.
The flight-engineer, who was newly rated for that aircraft, failed to detect the error and pass the information on to the pilots.
The plane came down on its nose, but did not require emergency evacuation.
Ansett has now appointed an air force commander as its new operational safety director.
AUSTUDY ANOMALY TO BE EXAMINED
The Federal Government agrees with the Democrats that it's outdated to class students up to the age of 25 as dependants.
In the Budget the Coalition extended the means and assets test for Austudy by three years.

Democrats Senator Natasha Stott Despoja says this may extend until the student is 30 because if they enrol before their 25th birthday, in a degree that can take up to six years, they'll be assessed on their family's income at the time of enrolment.
Employment and Education minister Amanda Vanstone's office says the anomaly will be examined.
GREENPEACE SAYS IT'S NOT BETRAYING PRINCIPLES
Greenpeace says its position remains that the only acceptable number of dolphins that should be killed are zero.
The Organisation has supported a plan to allow dolphin-deadly tuna to be sold in the US.
In the interests of free trade, the Clinton Administration is opening its market to previously banned tuna.
Countries wanting to be part of the deal will have to agree to overhaul their tuna-fishing practices, but not immediately.
Greenpeace Australia's Susan Cavanaugh says while dolphins will continue to be killed in the short term, in the long-term they'll be saved.
DOLE DIARY EXEMPTIONS WIDENED
The Federal Government has agreed to widen exemptions for unemployed people for its job-seekers diary after a union ban on the diary has been in place for two months.

Department of Social Security union members maintained the dole diary, requiring new applicants for unemployment benefits to detail job search activities, was designed to unfairly cut the number of people receiving benefits.
Unionists will vote tomorrow on a deal providing for extra exemptions.

The exemptions will be for people not able to understand or comply with the diary requirements, incapable of filling in the diary because of psychiatric problems or substance abuse or where it's not possible to verify with the employer that someone has made contact about a job.
NEW CORKS TO TAKE FUN OUT OF CHAMPERS
A new type of cork for champagne bottles could take some of the fun out of opening a bottle of bubbly.
The cork, produced in France, deflates when activated and can even be used to re-seal the bottle.
The assistant editor of New Scientist magazine, Vern Field, says the new cork could be good news for people who don't like the pressure behind traditional champagne corks.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
